metadata.title: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity responsive to plasmapheresis and immunosuppression.
metadata.abstract: The stiff-man syndrome is reported in a 55-year-old woman who also had signs of severe bulbar musculature hypercontraction. These clinical features correspond to the progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity syndrome. Diazepam was minimally beneficial, but after treatment with plasmapheresis and corticosteroids, she was still asymptomatic when seen 5 years later.

The stiff-man syndrome is reported in a 55-year-old 
woman who also had signs of severe bulbar musculature 
hypercontraction. These clinical features correspond to 
the progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity syndrome. 
Diazepam was minimally beneficial, but after treatment 
with plasmapheresis and corticosteroids, she was still 
asymptomatic when seen 5 years later. 
Fogan L. Progressive encephalomyelitis 
with rigidity responsive to 
plasmapheresis and immunosuppression. 
Ann Neurol 1996;40:45 1-453 
In 1971, Kasperek and Zebrowski [l] described a pa- 
tient in whom they diagnosed the stiff-man syndrome 
(SMS) and encephalomyelitis; at autopsy, inflamma- 
tion extended into the lower brainstem and spinal cord, 
which correlated with clinical deafness, vertical nystag- 
mus, and oculomotor paresis. Similar patients who had 
marked limb and truncal rigidity, severe spasms pro- 
voked by sensory or emotional stimuli, and autopsy 
findings of brainstem pathology with mild pleocytosis 
and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein elevation were 
described in 1973 [2] and 1976 [3]. Whiteley and col- 
leagues [3] referred to this illness as progressive enceph- 
alomyelitis with rigidity syndrome (PEMWRS). 
Our patient was first seen for fluctuating severe hyp- 
ercontraction of cranial nerve-innervated musculature 
3 months before the limbs and trunk became rigid. 
Total ophthalmoplegia developed, and she required 
gastrostomy feedings. Diazepam was only initially ef- 
fective for our patient, and successful treatment by 
plasmapheresis and immunosuppression was given. She 
remained asymptomatic when seen 5 years later. 
Case Report 
A 55-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA) 
was admitted to the hospital in late February 1989 for dehy-

dration secondary to 3 weeks of dysphagia and continuous 
diplopia; she was unable to swallow saliva. Penicillamine was 
stopped after a 10-year course when hydroxychloroquine was 
substituted 4 months earlier. 
At physical examination, the patient was alert and had 
multiaxial diplopia with mild ptosis in the right eye more 
than the left. Secretions were pooled in the pharynx, and 
hyperactive gag reflex was present. Tone and strength were 
normal; deep tendon reflexes were brisk except for trace ankle 
jerks, and plantar reflexes were equivocal. Sensory and cere- 
bellar test results were normal. Computed tomography (CT) 
and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head 
without contrast were normal. 
Intravenous edrophonium chloride resulted in no change. 
Routine laboratory test results were normal. Results of tests 
for anti-striational muscle antibody, anti-acetylcholine recep- 
tor antibody, and anti-nuclear antibodies were negative. 
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 50 mm/hr; CSF fluid 
was normal, including IgG synthesis and myelin basic pro- 
rein, and no oligoclonal bands were present. Esophagoscopy 
showed cricopharyngeal spasm. 
In mid-March 1989, a feeding gastrostomy tube was 
placed, and she was discharged without improvement. Dys- 
phagia and diplopia slowly resolved, and her gastrostomy 
tube was removed in May. 
In late June, she was readmitted because right leg spasms 
of 1-week duration caused gait problems and falling episodes 
with resultant right shoulder fracture and laceration. A teta- 
nus booster vaccination was administered. Intermittent 
multiaxial diplopia had returned without other central ner- 
vous system (CNS) symptoms. She had focal hypertonia with 
intermittent spasms of the right leg exacerbated by passive 
and active manipulation; generalized hyperactive deep ten- 
don reflexes and right knee clonus with equivocal plantar 
signs; and intermittent extensor spasms of the right leg more 
than of the left with no arm spasms. No percussion myoto- 
nia, myokymia, or fasciculations were seen. Gait was severely 
hampered by right leg stiffness. The spasms abated during 
sleep. Head CT, neck MRI, neck x-ray, and complete mye- 
lography results were normal without odontoid subluxation. 
Beads of sweat appeared on the left foreleg; none appeared 
on the right. In mid-July, she was discharged with persistent 
diplopia, but no dysphagia, and with painful right leg rigidity 
that was highly touch and movement stimulus sensitive. A 
urinary catheter was necessary, even though a cystometro- 
gram was normal. 
Two weeks later, the patient was readmitted for recurrent 
severe dysphagia; diplopia and painful right leg extensor 
spasms persisted. Electromyography (EMG) results revealed 
continuous motor unit discharges at rest simultaneously from 
the right leg flexors and extensors (eg, gastrocnemius and 
tibialis anterior); light touch to the leg consistently exagger- 
ated this response and increased both the number of motor 
units present and their intensity. 
Fewer of these same abnormalities were observed in the 
left leg, even fewer in the right arm, and only minimal such 
changes in the left arm. No sharp waves, fibrillations, fascicu- 
lations, or myopathic changes were seen. No bursts of motor 
unit action potentials firing at 150 to 300 Hz for several 
seconds nor grouped discharges of motor unit action poten- 
tials recurring regularly at rates up to 60 Hz were observed. 
Copyright 0 1996 by the American Neurological Association 451

Neuromyotonia and myokymia were therefore excluded from 
the diagnosis (41. 
Diazepam, 15 mg orally four times daily, markedly dimin- 
ished extensor spasms. EMG repeated 3 weeks later while 
the patient was receiving diazepam, 15 mg three times daily, 
showed substantial improvement. Although diplopia per- 
sisted, the patient could walk with a walker, swallow, and 
was continent at discharge in mid-Aug,ust. Medications in- 
cluded the above diazepam dosage and prednisone, 7.5 mg 
every other day, which she had taken for years as an antiar- 
thritic agent. 
In late August, nausea and vomiting precluded taking di- 
azepam, and the patient was readmitted because of severe 
trunk rigidity, urinary retention, near total ophthalmoplegia, 
trismus, and inability to swallow. Intravenous administration 
of 5 mg diazepam had no effect, and pulmonary arrest neces- 
sitated ventilator-dependent intubation, later requiring tra- 
cheotomy. Hypercontraction did not respond to up to 80 
mg diazepam daily. Dantrolene sodium, carbamazepine, car- 
bidopa-levodopa, and phenytoin were ineffective. Forced 
ductions demonstrated that the ophthalmoplegia was second- 
ary to hypercontraction of all extraocular muscles. 
In late September, plasmapheresis was initiated; six treat- 
ments during 2 weeks produced graclual improvement in 
stiffness, ophthalmoplegia, and dysphagia; ventilation sup- 
port was discontinued. Two weeks later, prednisone was in- 
creased from 7.5 mg daily to 60 mg daily. A hyperosmolar, 
nonketotic sate developed, which was treated with insulin. 
Some paranoia occurred but decreased when prednisone dos- 
age was decreased to 20 mg twice daily. 
A left quadriceps muscle biopsy demonstrated angular and 
fascicular atrophy suggesting denervation. Fascia1 and peri- 
mysial alkaline and acid phosphatase reactivity indicated vas- 
cular or fascia1 inflammation, or both “but no inflammatory 
cells were observed). Biopsy results suggested inflammatory 
vasculopathy or faciitis associated with RA. Serum antibodies 
against GABAergic synapses were not detected in pre- and 
postplasmapheresis sera (courtesy of Ilr Pietro De Camilli 
and Dr Michele Solimena, Yale School of Medicine, utilizing 
brain tissue in an immunocytochemical assay) [5]. In mid- 
November, the patient was discharged. She had full extraocu- 
lar movements but still had diplopia. She could swallow, 
walk, and had no spasms of hypertoniii. She was taking aza- 
thioprine, 75 mg daily; prednisone, 20 mg twice daily; and 
diazepam, 5 mg twice daily. 
In February 1990, the patient was doing her own house- 
work and had gained 8.1 kg. She was cuishingoid. She had 
full extraocular movements but wore an eye patch to obviate 
persistent diplopia. She was eating and walking well, and she 
was continent. Medications included diazepam, 20 mg daily; 
azathioprine, 50 mg daily; and prednisone, 15 mg daily. She 
was no longer diabetic. 
In 1994, the patient still had no hypercontraction symp- 
toms, signs, or diplopia. Medications included prednisone, 
5 mg daily; azathioprine, 50 mg daily; and no diazepam. 
Discussion 
The etiology of SMS and PEMWRS is unknown, but 
the literature suggests that both are autoimmune disor- 
ders of the CNS directed against suprasegmental or 
spinal inhibitory GABAergic neurons [6, 71. Diazepam 
facilitates GABA action and inhibits continuous motor 
activity. Plasmapheresis has been reported therapeutic 
for SMS in some centers [8, 91 but not in others [lo, 
111. Intravenous immune globulin also can be useful 
[ 121. Attempts to treat PEMWRS with parenteral diaz- 
epam, oral baclofen, and oral prednisone [13] and with 
intravenous methylprednisolone and oral phenytoin 
[14] have met with mild to moderate success. Plasma- 
pheresis and immunosuppression were effective for our 
patient and apparently alleviated symptoms up to 5 
years later. 
Paraneoplastic pathogenesis of SMS and PEMWRS 
has been suggested in a report [15] of SMS associated 
with oat cell carcinoma in which perivascular lympho- 
cytic cuffing was found in the putamen, lower medulla, 
and white matter as well as anterior horns in multilev- 
els of the spinal cord. These changes are typical of en- 
cephalomyelitis associated with cancer, and lympho- 
cytic perivascular cuffing has been similarly found in 
SMS and PEMWRS without associated neoplasm [l- 
31. The mechanism causing this cuffing is not precisely 
known but is probably immunologic or infectious. 
It is of interest that this patient had been on penicil- 
lamine for the previous decade, a drug that can pro- 
voke autoimmune disorders such as myasthenia gravis 
and neuromyotonia [16]. Testing was not done for ex- 
tinction of electrical and contractile activity in the pres- 
ence of myoneural junction block, motor nerve block, 
or general anesthesia, because the EMG responses and 
the lack of benefit of therapeutic levels of dilantin and 
carbamazepine challenged the diagnosis of neuromyo- 
tonia. 
Our patient’s clinical course of waxing and waning 
rigidity discounts tetanus but strongly supports an 
SMS-PEMWRS continuum. Plasmapheresis and im- 
munosuppression may be dramatically effective and 
should be used despite lack of knowledge about this 
disorder’s causal mechanism. 
Anthony Verity, MD, University of California School of Medicine 
at Los Angeles, provided pathology consultation; Pietro De Camilli, 
MD, and Michele Solimena, MD, Yale University School of Medi- 
cine, consulted on antibody assay. W. Gerald Wythe, MD, Depart- 
ment of Physical Medicine, performed EMG examinations, and Bal- 
asubrahmanyan Shantha, MD, provided primary care support: both 
are at Kaiser Permanente Medical Center, Panorama City, Califor-

A 44-year-old man developed blurry vision, photosensi- 
tivity, orthostasis, constipation, and acrodysesthesias after 
a febrile illness. The neurologic examination and ancillary 
studies were consistent with a dysautonomic small fiber 
neuropathy. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) contained 
both Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA and antibody to 
EBV. This is the first report of an acute autonomic neu- 
ropathy with documented EBV infection in CSF. 
Bennett JL, Mahalingam R, Wellish MC, 
Gilden DH. Epstein-Barr virus-associated 
acute autonomic neuropathy. 
Ann Neurol 1996;40:453-455 
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a ubiquitous human her- 
pesvirus. Neurologic complications include meningi- 
tis, meningoencephalitis, central nervous system 
lymphoma, transverse myelitis, psychiatric disorders, 
and polyneuropathies [ 11. Cranial nerve and peripheral 
polyneuropathies have been associated with EBV by 
the development of EBV-specific or heterophile anti- 
bodies in serum during acute disease [2-71. Three 
other reports have documented concurrent acute auto- 
nomic neuropathy (AAN) [3, 4, 71. EBV DNA and 
antibody to EBV have never been identified in cerebro- 
spinal fluid (CSF) of patients with either the Guillain- 
Bark syndrome or AAN. Thus, we looked for antibody 
to EBV and EBV DNA in CSF of a patient with AAN. 
Case History 
In June 1995, a 44-year-old man awakened with burning 
pain and exquisite sensitivity, throughout his body, to cold 
water or light touch, particularly when dressing. He noted 
pupillary enlargement, trouble focusing, decreased taste sen- 
sation, a longer time to urinate, and constipation, but no 
light-headedness or sexual dysfunction. He lost 40 Ib within 
a month. Past history was unremarkable. 
Two months later, examination revealed a recent burn on 
the right forearm, which the patient called inadvertent. Re-

carbamazepine challenged the diagnosis of neuromyo- 
tonia. 
Our patient’s clinical course of waxing and waning 
rigidity discounts tetanus but strongly supports an 
SMS-PEMWRS continuum. Plasmapheresis and im- 
munosuppression may be dramatically effective and 
should be used despite lack of knowledge about this 
disorder’s causal mechanism.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a ubiquitous human her- 
pesvirus. Neurologic complications include meningi- 
tis, meningoencephalitis, central nervous system 
lymphoma, transverse myelitis, psychiatric disorders, 
and polyneuropathies [ 11. Cranial nerve and peripheral 
polyneuropathies have been associated with EBV by 
the development of EBV-specific or heterophile anti- 
bodies in serum during acute disease [2-71. Three 
other reports have documented concurrent acute auto- 
nomic neuropathy (AAN) [3, 4, 71. EBV DNA and 
antibody to EBV have never been identified in cerebro- 
spinal fluid (CSF) of patients with either the Guillain- 
Bark syndrome or AAN. Thus, we looked for antibody 
to EBV and EBV DNA in CSF of a patient with AAN.
